title: Code Review Bench: An Automated Benchmark for Evaluating the Software Factory
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: A staged data pipeline turns raw public event streams into judged, stratified, continuously refreshed rankings of tools.
layout: 6 panels in 2 rows, left-to-right, numbered stages joined by arrows
description: A two-row flow of six rounded gray cards linked by chevron arrows. Row one has 1 Discover, 2 Enrich and 3 Assemble. Discover shows a GitHub logo above an isometric box with bot icons, and the caption '4.1M+ PRs | 18 tools refreshed daily'. Dashed lines run from the bot icons into Enrich. Enrich lists data sources with checkmarks: review comments, inline comments, commits, review decisions and repo metadata. Assemble shows two stacks of cards, developer actions and bot suggestions, joined by a dotted line, with an 'Engagement Signals + dev actions + bot suggestions' pill row underneath. Row two has 4 Analyze, 5 Label and a results table. Analyze shows star ratings for precision, recall and F1, with an 'LLM Judge Examination' label. Label shows colored tag chips such as Java, Backend and Critical. The final card is a ranked leaderboard of F-score, precision and recall. The palette is black, purple and orange-red accents on gray.
caption: The Code Review Bench pipeline: (1) Discover PRs via BigQuery, (2) Enrich via GitHub API, (3) Assemble bot--developer timelines, (4) Analyze with LLM judge, (5) Label for stratification.
abstract: As AI agents ship more code with minimal human oversight, code review becomes the critical quality-control checkpoint -- but one without a reliable, objective verifier: review quality is nuanced and ultimately a judgment call by the PR author. Existing benchmarks are structurally misaligned with this: annotators are third-party reviewers, like the bots they evaluate, not the PR authors who actually decide what to fix. They also rely on small, static issue sets that require full re-evaluation as tools update, limiting how frequently progress can be tracked. We introduce CodeReviewBench, built on a fundamentally different signal: revealed developer preferences -- if a developer acts on a bot's suggestion, we treat it as useful; if they ignore it, we do not. This signal is mined daily from the public GitHub event stream, yielding 500K+ judged PRs across 18 tools, and refreshes continuously as tools evolve. We validate the developer preference against an independent offline benchmark: the two agree on precision rankings and independently detect the same product updates within days of vendor releases. Together, these form the benchmark.
